title: Redwood x NorthBridge Bank — GenAI platform discovery
topics: Current GenAI stack and why NorthBridge is re-evaluating inference
Regulatory/compliance constraints (GLBA/FFIEC), data residency, retention, auditability
Deployment requirements (private/VPC), network controls, and key management
Success criteria: latency, throughput, cost, reliability, audit logs
Next steps: security review + product demo + architecture exchange
summary: NorthBridge is standing up a centralized GenAI platform for internal apps (contact center assist, policy/KB Q&A, and some doc summarization). They are currently using a mix of Azure OpenAI for prototypes and a small internal GPU cluster for experiments, but need a production inference path that meets bank security requirements (US-only residency, customer-managed keys, detailed audit logs, strict retention, SSO/RBAC) and provides predictable performance/cost. Redwood positioned Dedicated vs Private deployments for regulated workloads, discussed audit logging and KMS/HSM integrations at a high level, and aligned on initial success metrics (p95 latency, throughput at steady load, cost per 1k tokens, and operational visibility). Next steps are to schedule a formal security review (evidence pack under NDA) and a technical demo focused on Redwood Console, deployment topology, and logging/export patterns.
next_steps: Redwood to send regulated workloads Security FAQ + evidence pack index (NDA gated for SOC 2 report) to Megan
Schedule 60-min security review with Dr. Aisha Rahman’s team / Naomi Feldman + Olga Petrov (target: next week)
Schedule technical demo (Dedicated vs Private, routing/fallback, Console dashboards) with Jordan + Tom (target: this week/early next week)
NorthBridge to share a redacted target architecture + network constraints (ingress/egress, allowed regions, preferred cloud) and success criteria for first use case
Redwood to follow up with a proposed 2-week benchmark/pilot outline and mutual action plan template
action_items: Avery Johnson — Email recap + proposed times for demo and security review — Due 2025-05-07
Markus Klein — Share high-level reference architecture options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; VPC patterns) — Due 2025-05-08
Megan Liu — Confirm whether SOC 2 Type II report requires NDA and who can sign — Due 2025-05-09
Tom Harrington — Provide NorthBridge allowed outbound endpoints / egress requirements and preferred log destination (Splunk/S3/etc.) — Due 2025-05-09
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Redwood x NorthBridge Bank — GenAI platform discovery
Date: 2025-05-06
Time: 10:03 AM – 10:50 AM ET
Duration: 47 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Jordan Patel (NorthBridge Bank, Director GenAI Platform)
- Megan Liu (NorthBridge Bank, InfoSec Architect)
- Tom Harrington (NorthBridge Bank, Cloud Platform Lead)
- Sanjay Rao (NorthBridge Bank, Head of Data Engineering)

-----

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Hey everyone, thanks for making the time. I’m Avery, I run North America accounts at Redwood for— specifically the platform teams. Markus is here with me, he’s our solutions engineering lead.

[00:10] Markus Klein: Hey all.

[00:12] Jordan Patel: Hi, Jordan here. Thanks. We’ve got Megan from security, Tom from cloud platform, and Sanjay from data engineering.

[00:20] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Um, goal for today is just discovery. We’ll do intros, understand what you’re building, constraints, and then if it makes sense we’ll tee up a security review and a deeper demo.

[00:31] Jordan Patel: Yep, that’s exactly what we need.

[00:34] Avery Johnson: Cool. Jordan, do you want to start with like, what prompted the call? Where are you in terms of gen AI platform work?

[00:43] Jordan Patel: Sure. So— we have a few teams that have been prototyping with, honestly, whatever they can. Mostly Azure OpenAI because it’s easy and procurement already exists. But we’re getting pressure now to centralize. We’re calling it the GenAI Platform. We’re trying to provide a standard interface for internal apps.

[01:01] Jordan Patel: Primary use cases are internal: contact center agent assist, knowledge base Q&A, and document summarization for, like, policy and procedure docs. Some folks are trying to do transaction narrative summarization, but that gets into sensitive data.

[01:17] Avery Johnson: Got it. And the reason you’re evaluating Redwood is— compliance? performance? cost? all of the above?

[01:24] Jordan Patel: All of the above, yeah. We have very strict requirements. We’re a bank. So data residency, audit logs, retention controls, and then predictability. Azure is— fine but expensive and we don’t really get the knobs we want. And self-hosting… we tried. It’s painful.

[01:41] Tom Harrington: Yeah, we spun up vLLM on a k8s cluster, like, an AKS cluster, and it works until it doesn’t. The batching, the GPU utilization, then someone changes a model and everything breaks.

[01:55] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s a common story.

[01:57] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. Before we go deeper, can I ask: are you primarily Azure as a cloud, or multi-cloud?

[02:05] Tom Harrington: Predominantly Azure. But we have some AWS pockets. And we have a private data center footprint. For this GenAI thing, direction is “cloud-first but not public internet.” Like, private connectivity.

[02:20] Megan Liu: And US-only. No non-US processing. That’s not negotiable.

[02:25] Avery Johnson: Understood. We can talk about that. Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. For regulated workloads, typically we see Dedicated in a single region with strict controls, or Private in your VPC, or on-prem for certain cases. We’ll map that to your requirements.

[02:43] Jordan Patel: Okay.

[02:45] Avery Johnson: Can you describe the current “stack” end-to-end? Like app calls, orchestration, where prompts live, logging, etc.

[02:55] Sanjay Rao: I can jump in. For prototypes, teams are using LangChain or sometimes just direct SDK calls. Prompts are in GitHub repos. Data is mostly in Snowflake and some in CosmosDB. For the support use case, they pull content from our internal KB, it’s in SharePoint and Confluence, and they do retrieval.

[03:15] Sanjay Rao: Logging is messy. Some teams log prompts, some don’t. That’s a big concern. We need consistent audit trails.

[03:23] Megan Liu: Yeah, and “don’t log sensitive data” is the rule, but enforcement is inconsistent. We need a platform-level control.

[03:31] Markus Klein: When you say audit trail, do you mean user access to the system, admin actions, model calls, or like, all of it?

[03:38] Megan Liu: Ideally all of it. Minimum is admin actions and model invocation metadata. We also need the ability to prove who accessed what, and when. We have to answer that question.

[03:50] Tom Harrington: And we need export. We centralize logs in Splunk. Some teams use Azure Monitor, but Splunk is the system of record.

[03:59] Avery Johnson: Got it. And is there a retention policy you’re aiming for? Like, 30 days, 90 days?

[04:05] Megan Liu: Depends. But for platform logs, we often do 90 days hot, then archive. For prompts/responses, it’s tricky. We likely want “no retention by default” for content, or very short retention with explicit approval.

[04:19] Avery Johnson: That’s helpful.

[04:21] Jordan Patel: We’re also trying to align with FFIEC guidance, GLBA. Our model vendor needs to support— you know, encryption at rest and in transit, key management. Preferably customer-managed keys.

[04:36] Markus Klein: CMK / BYOK, yep.

[04:38] Jordan Patel: Right.

[04:40] Avery Johnson: Okay. Let me ask about where you are in terms of rollout timeline. Is this exploratory, or do you have a date?

[04:48] Jordan Patel: We have pressure to have something production-ready in Q3. So, like, 8 to 12 weeks for vendor selection and a pilot. But security review can take a while.

[05:00] Megan Liu: Security review will take as long as it takes. But we can move quickly if the vendor is prepared.

[05:06] Avery Johnson: That’s fair. We’ve been running a regulated workloads motion, so we have a packaged security FAQ and evidence pack process. We can walk you through. We won’t over-claim anything.

[05:17] Megan Liu: Good.

[05:19] Avery Johnson: Markus, do you want to ask the technical questions on performance/SLOs?

[05:24] Markus Klein: Sure. Jordan, what are your success criteria? Like, for the first use case. Is it a chat experience? latency sensitive? throughput?

[05:34] Jordan Patel: For agent assist, it’s interactive. We’re targeting sub-2 seconds time-to-first-token, and then, I don’t know, responses within 5 to 8 seconds. But we need predictable p95. Not average.

[05:49] Tom Harrington: Also concurrency. We have call center peaks. It’s not massive like consumer scale, but we might have a few hundred concurrent sessions in the future.

[05:58] Markus Klein: Great. And model size? Do you have a preference? Like Llama 3 70B, Mixtral, smaller models?

[06:06] Jordan Patel: We’re evaluating. For now, most teams use GPT-4o via Azure because quality. But security doesn’t love that. We’re open to open models if quality is good.

[06:19] Megan Liu: “Security doesn’t love that” is an understatement. We need contractual and technical guarantees.

[06:24] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[06:26] Markus Klein: Redwood’s platform supports a catalog of open models and we can pin versions. For regulated environments, we often see customers start with something like Llama 3.1 70B class (or smaller) depending on the workload. But we’d want to benchmark with your prompts.

[06:42] Tom Harrington: The other part is cost. We’re getting hammered on per-token cost right now.

[06:48] Avery Johnson: Yep. We can talk unit economics. We also have tooling in the Console that shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and knobs around batching/caching/quantization.

[06:59] Sanjay Rao: Do you do embeddings too? We’d like a single platform.

[07:03] Markus Klein: Yes, embeddings and reranking as well. Same API surface.

[07:08] Jordan Patel: Okay.

[07:10] Avery Johnson: Megan, can we dig into the compliance constraints list? Just so we don’t waste time. What are the “hard no” items?

[07:18] Megan Liu: Sure. Hard no: data leaving the US. Hard no: data being used to train vendor models. Hard no: lack of audit logging for admin access and system changes. We also need SSO, preferably SAML with Okta, and role based access controls.

[07:36] Megan Liu: Encryption in transit TLS 1.2+, encryption at rest. For keys, we strongly prefer customer-managed keys, and ideally HSM backed. We use Azure Key Vault and on-prem HSM for certain things.

[07:51] Tom Harrington: Also private networking. We can’t call a public endpoint across the internet. We can do private link type connectivity. Or VPC/VNet.

[08:01] Avery Johnson: Great. Redwood Dedicated can be configured with private connectivity options, and Redwood Private is deployed into your VPC/VNet with customer-managed networking. We can cover both. The right choice depends on how much control you need and how quickly you want to move.

[08:19] Jordan Patel: What’s the difference in plain English?

[08:22] Avery Johnson: Dedicated is reserved capacity that Redwood operates— isolated compute, predictable throughput, but still managed by us. Private is where the control plane and inference plane are deployed in your environment, so network and data boundaries are yours. More control, more involved setup.

[08:40] Jordan Patel: Okay.

[08:41] Megan Liu: For anything with customer data, Private is likely required. For internal-only with no customer info, maybe Dedicated.

[08:50] Sanjay Rao: Even internal can have customer identifiers though.

[08:53] Jordan Patel: Yeah, it’s messy.

[08:56] Markus Klein: Often teams define a first pilot use case that is “lower risk” to start. Like internal policy Q&A with curated content, no PII. Then expand.

[09:06] Jordan Patel: That’s probably how we’ll do it.

[09:09] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[09:11] Markus Klein: Megan, on audit logging— what do you expect in terms of fields? Like, user ID, request ID, model version, timestamp, admin actions?

[09:20] Megan Liu: Yeah. User identity (from SSO), source IP, action type, resource. For model calls we want at least metadata: who invoked, what model, tokens, latency. Ideally we can choose to not store prompt content.

[09:37] Markus Klein: Yep. We have audit logs that capture control plane actions and can include request metadata. For prompt/response content, we can talk about retention policies and redaction. We don’t recommend storing sensitive content unless you have a policy.

[09:51] Tom Harrington: Can you export those logs to Splunk? Or do we have to pull?

[09:56] Markus Klein: In Private deployments, you can route logs to your own sinks. In managed modes, we have export patterns— we can review specifics in the security review and in a technical deep dive.

[10:10] Avery Johnson: I don’t want to promise a specific integration on this call without confirming your exact requirements. But yes, exporting to common SIEM/log systems is a common ask.

[10:20] Megan Liu: Appreciate that.

[10:22] Avery Johnson: Also, for SOC 2 and evidence, we can provide an evidence pack under NDA. That includes things like our SOC 2 report process, diagrams, and policy statements.

[10:34] Megan Liu: Okay. We’ll need that.

[10:36] Jordan Patel: Can I ask a naive question. If we do Private, who patches it? Like, who owns upgrades?

[10:44] Markus Klein: Good question. Typically Redwood provides the software and guidance, and we can offer support tiers. Depending on the package, we help coordinate upgrades. But because it’s in your environment, your team will own some operational parts. We’ll be transparent about that.

[11:01] Tom Harrington: We have a platform SRE team, but we don’t want to become an ML infra company.

[11:07] Markus Klein: Understood.

[11:10] Avery Johnson: That’s actually why most teams choose Dedicated for as long as possible, unless regulatory boundaries force Private.

[11:18] Megan Liu: Boundaries will force it for certain workloads.

[11:21] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[11:22] Jordan Patel: Another question: do you support multiple regions? Like disaster recovery.

[11:28] Avery Johnson: Yes. In Dedicated and Private you can design for regional isolation / DR. The details depend on your architecture and what “active-active” vs “active-passive” means for you.

[11:39] Tom Harrington: We’d likely start single region, with a DR plan. Regulators will ask.

[11:45] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[11:47] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about the first workload. Agent assist: is it RAG? Are you calling tools? Or just chat?

[11:55] Jordan Patel: It’s RAG plus some tool calls. Like, retrieve knowledge, maybe open a ticket, maybe pull customer profile. But we’re cautious about tool actions.

[12:05] Sanjay Rao: We also want structured outputs. Like JSON. Because the downstream system expects that.

[12:11] Markus Klein: We support structured output and tool/function calling patterns. We can demo that.

[12:16] Avery Johnson: Great.

[12:18] Megan Liu: Tool calling is scary. If the model can trigger actions, we need strong controls and audit.

[12:25] Markus Klein: Totally. Usually you implement approval workflows, allow lists, and you audit tool invocations separately. The platform can help with observability.

[12:35] Tom Harrington: What about rate limiting and quotas? We need to avoid runaway costs.

[12:41] Avery Johnson: Built-in. You can set quotas and per-route limits. And we can provide budget alerts.

[12:48] Jordan Patel: Okay.

[12:50] Avery Johnson: I want to be mindful of time. Maybe let’s align on what a successful next two weeks looks like. For us, it’s: 1) security review to make sure we can meet the minimum bar, and 2) a demo tailored to your architecture, and then 3) define a pilot.

[13:08] Jordan Patel: Yes. That’s what we need.

[13:10] Megan Liu: I’ll need your standard security questionnaire answers too. Like encryption, access control, incident response.

[13:18] Avery Johnson: We have a security FAQ tailored for regulated workloads. It’s sales-ready but accurate. For deeper items, our security team can join the review.

[13:29] Megan Liu: Okay.

[13:31] Markus Klein: On the pilot— would you want us to run a benchmark with your prompts? Or do you want to integrate first?

[13:37] Jordan Patel: Benchmark first. We can provide a prompt set, redacted. But we need to be careful about what leaves.

[13:46] Megan Liu: We can share synthetic prompts to start. Real prompts might require approvals.

[13:52] Markus Klein: Totally fine. Synthetic prompts still help for latency/throughput.

[13:57] Tom Harrington: And network wise, if we’re benchmarking, how would we connect? We can’t just call an endpoint from a laptop.

[14:06] Avery Johnson: For early benchmarking, we often do it on Redwood’s side with non-sensitive prompts. For anything with sensitive data, we’d wait until a Private or dedicated environment with the right connectivity.

[14:19] Megan Liu: Okay.

[14:20] Jordan Patel: Makes sense.

[14:22] Avery Johnson: Can I ask: who else needs to be involved to make a decision? Procurement, risk, architecture review board?

[14:30] Jordan Patel: Eventually procurement and vendor risk. But first we need security buy-in. And our architecture review board, yes.

[14:39] Tom Harrington: The ARB will ask about network topology, dependencies, how it fits with our identity provider, logging.

[14:46] Markus Klein: We can provide reference architectures. We can also join an ARB meeting if needed.

[14:52] Avery Johnson: Great.

[14:54] Megan Liu: Also, we’ll ask about data retention. We can’t have “we keep your data forever.”

[15:00] Avery Johnson: Understood. Redwood’s approach is configurable retention and we can align to your policy. We’ll cover specifics in the security review and in the contract language. We won’t claim “HIPAA-ready” or anything like that— we stick to what we can prove.

[15:15] Megan Liu: Thank you.

[15:17] Jordan Patel: Another thing: model updates. How do we prevent a silent model change?

[15:23] Markus Klein: Great question. We support version pinning and controlled rollouts— canary, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You can hold a model version constant until you approve.

[15:37] Jordan Patel: That’s important.

[15:39] Sanjay Rao: And evals? We’re building some eval harness.

[15:42] Markus Klein: We integrate with eval workflows. At minimum we can help you run regression tests tied to prompts.

[15:49] Avery Johnson: We can show that in the Console.

[15:52] Tom Harrington: One more question: Do you sit on top of Nvidia? Like what’s your infra.

[15:57] Markus Klein: We run across multiple GPU types depending on deployment. For Private, it’s your hardware or cloud choice. For Dedicated/Hosted, we manage the fleet. The key is the runtime optimizations— batching, KV cache management, kernel selection— to keep latency low while controlling cost.

[16:15] Tom Harrington: KV cache… yeah our team has been fighting that.

[16:18] Markus Klein: Yeah, same.

[16:20] Avery Johnson: Can we dig into identity? You mentioned Okta. Any SCIM provisioning requirements?

[16:27] Megan Liu: SAML is the main thing. SCIM is nice-to-have. We need least privilege. And we need to be able to remove access quickly.

[16:36] Avery Johnson: Great. We’ll cover SSO/RBAC. I’ll loop in our security team for the detailed questions.

[16:43] Jordan Patel: What about data classification? Like can you guarantee prompts aren’t used for training.

[16:49] Avery Johnson: Yes, we do not use customer data to train models. We can provide contractual assurances. For the exact data handling and retention, we’ll align in the security review.

[17:02] Megan Liu: Contractual language matters.

[17:04] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[17:06] Markus Klein: Also on “who can see data” internally— we’ll cover access controls and auditability. In Private, your team has full control. In managed, there are restricted access paths with logging.

[17:21] Megan Liu: That’s what I’ll want to see.

[17:24] Avery Johnson: Totally.

[17:26] (crosstalk)

[17:27] Jordan Patel: Sorry, go ahead Tom.

[17:29] Tom Harrington: I was just going to say— outbound internet restrictions. If the system needs to call home to Redwood, that can be a blocker.

[17:37] Markus Klein: For Private, there are options for restricted egress depending on the package. We’ll want to understand what’s permitted. Sometimes it’s a control plane connectivity requirement; sometimes it can be done with private endpoints.

[17:51] Avery Johnson: Let’s capture that as a specific question for the demo and security review.

[17:56] Tom Harrington: Yeah.

[17:57] Avery Johnson: Okay. We have about 30 minutes left. I’d like to ask a few qualification questions and then we’ll do next steps.

[18:05] Avery Johnson: Budget-wise, are you thinking usage-based, or do you need reserved capacity?

[18:11] Jordan Patel: For bank, we prefer predictable. So reserved capacity is easier.

[18:16] Tom Harrington: And we need an SLA.

[18:18] Avery Johnson: Great. Dedicated and Private both align with that.

[18:22] Avery Johnson: Implementation ownership— who will be hands-on for a pilot? Tom’s team? Jordan’s team? Someone else?

[18:29] Jordan Patel: Tom’s team for networking and platform. My team for app integration. Sanjay for data pipelines.

[18:36] Avery Johnson: Great. Markus can be your technical point person. We can set up a shared channel during pilot.

[18:44] Markus Klein: Yep.

[18:46] Avery Johnson: What about legal/vendor risk timeline? If we hit go, how long does it take to onboard a vendor?

[18:54] Jordan Patel: Best case 6 weeks. Worst case… longer.

[18:58] Megan Liu: Vendor risk needs SOC reports, pen test info, incident response policy, DPA addendum. We have standard templates.

[19:10] Avery Johnson: Understood. We can support that.

[19:13] Markus Klein: On the technical side, do you have a preference between Azure and AWS for a Private deployment?

[19:20] Tom Harrington: Azure. But if you only support AWS…

[19:23] Avery Johnson: We support multiple environments. Let’s align in the demo.

[19:29] Jordan Patel: Can we talk about what you mean by “Private control plane”? Is it like we run your software in our VNet?

[19:36] Markus Klein: Yes, that’s essentially it. You run the inference stack inside your network boundary. There’s a management layer for updates/operations depending on your chosen model. We’ll show a reference diagram.

[19:50] Megan Liu: Okay.

[19:52] Avery Johnson: Let’s pause and ask: is there anything you’ve heard so far that’s a mismatch?

[19:58] Jordan Patel: Not yet.

[20:00] Megan Liu: I need details before I say yes.

[20:03] Avery Johnson: Totally fair.

[20:05] Tom Harrington: I want to see how you handle logging and egress.

[20:08] Avery Johnson: Great.

[20:10] Markus Klein: Jordan, any models that are off limits? Some banks have policy restrictions.

[20:16] Jordan Patel: We can use open source if we can show it’s controlled and we’re not sending data to random endpoints. For commercial APIs, it’s… complicated.

[20:27] Megan Liu: We need to control where the data goes and who can access it. That’s the main point.

[20:33] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[20:35] Avery Johnson: There was a mention of Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock. Are those still on the table as options? Or are you actively looking to move away?

[20:43] Jordan Patel: They’re on the table for lower-risk use cases. But for the platform long-term we want something we can run privately.

[20:52] Avery Johnson: Great. That aligns.

[20:54] Sanjay Rao: Quick one: do you do any prompt caching? Because we have repeated queries.

[20:59] Markus Klein: Yes, there are caching mechanisms, including prefix/KV caching patterns. But it’s workload dependent. We’ll talk about it when we see your traffic pattern.

[21:11] Sanjay Rao: Okay.

[21:13] Avery Johnson: I think it makes sense to move to next steps. Megan, can you share how you like to run security review? Is it a questionnaire first, or a call?

[21:24] Megan Liu: Usually we start with a call to understand architecture and scope. Then we share the questionnaire and request evidence. For SOC 2 we’ll need an NDA.

[21:35] Avery Johnson: Perfect. We’ll schedule a 60-minute security review. I’ll bring our security exec sponsor or compliance lead— likely Naomi Feldman and Olga Petrov— depending on availability.

[21:47] Megan Liu: Okay.

[21:48] Avery Johnson: And then separate 60-minute demo with Markus to focus on the product and architecture.

[21:56] Jordan Patel: Sounds good.

[21:58] Tom Harrington: Can the demo include the network diagram? Like, how the VPC thing works.

[22:02] Markus Klein: Yes. We’ll show reference architectures and what ports/paths are needed at a high level.

[22:10] Tom Harrington: Great.

[22:12] Avery Johnson: Awesome. Before we wrap, I’ll summarize what I heard, and you tell me if I missed anything.

[22:19] Avery Johnson: You’re building a centralized GenAI platform for internal apps. You’ve used Azure OpenAI for prototypes. You’ve tried self-hosted vLLM on k8s but it’s hard to make stable and cost efficient. You have strict requirements: US-only residency, no training on your data, private networking, SSO (Okta SAML), RBAC, audit logs with export to Splunk, and tight retention controls especially around prompt/response content.

[22:43] Avery Johnson: First success criteria are p95 latency for interactive agent assist (sub-2s TTFT target), predictable throughput, and cost control. And you’re aiming for vendor selection/pilot in the next 8-12 weeks, with production in Q3.

[22:59] Jordan Patel: Yes. That’s correct.

[23:01] Megan Liu: Yup.

[23:03] Tom Harrington: Sounds right.

[23:05] Avery Johnson: Great. Anything else?

[23:07] Sanjay Rao: Just that we need a path for embeddings and retrieval too, but not blocking for the first pilot.

[23:13] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[23:15] Markus Klein: And we’ll want a prompt set, even synthetic, to run a benchmark.

[23:19] Jordan Patel: Yes.

[23:21] Avery Johnson: Cool. I’ll send a recap email today with proposed times for both calls, and I’ll attach our security FAQ and the evidence pack index, with instructions for NDA for the SOC report.

[23:34] Megan Liu: Please do.

[23:35] Avery Johnson: Great. Thanks everyone.

[23:38] Jordan Patel: Thanks.

[23:39] Tom Harrington: Thanks.

[23:40] Markus Klein: Thanks all.

-----

Auto-generated (Fireflies)
Questions captured:
- Can Redwood support US-only data residency and private networking without public internet access?
- What audit log fields are available, and how can logs be exported to Splunk?
- How does Redwood handle customer-managed keys / HSM-backed KMS integrations?
- What are retention controls for prompts/responses vs metadata?
- What is the operational model for Redwood Private (patching/upgrades)?

End of transcript.
